subject: Estimating multidimensional a priori item parameters

messages.author: 684c2179d07b3fc3
messages.subject: Estimating multidimensional a priori item parameters
parts:
Hello,

I am on a journey learning MIRT as a complete beginner and have a better grasp on it after reading Reckase's textbook on the matter. 

However, I still have one major gap in my knowledge: where do the initial item parameters come from? I can find information regarding estimating item parameters for known thetas and estimating thetas with known item parameters, but this seems like a paradox.

How can I know the thetas of a group of examinees without first knowing the item parameters?

Let's assume I have already observed the traditional test results of 100 examinees for 20 questions each and want to construct a mirt model. How do I pick the parameters? An example shown on the mirtCAT github page is:

library("mirtCAT")
set.seed(1)

# multidimensional IRT model with simple structure (continuation from Example 2)
nitems <- 100
a <- rlnorm(nitems, .2, .3) # from Example 2
d <- runif(nitems, -3, 3)
g <- rep(0.2, nitems)

a <- matrix(c(a, numeric(nitems*2), rlnorm(nitems, .2, .3)), 200)
d <- c(d, runif(nitems, -3, 3))
g <- c(g, rep(0.2, nitems))

pars <- data.frame(a1 = a[,1], a2=a[,2], d = d, g = g)
head(pars)
pars[98:103, ]
tail(pars)

# correlation between traits
lc <- matrix(c(1,.6,.6,1), 2, 2)

mirt_object <- generate.mirt_object(pars, itemtype = "3PL",
                                    latent_covariance = lc)


It seems the item parameters are arbitrarily decided from distributions.

If anyone could explain what I am missing or point me toward a related thread that would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks all,
Peter

messages.author: b90ec12f746e359e
messages.subject: Re: Estimating multidimensional a priori item parameters
parts:
Hi Peter,

I am a beginner myself but I will try to answer, in case you have not found an answer already.

Item parameters come from the mirt package, which creates a mirt-type object based on data and some further options passed through the function. In the example that you have presented here the item parameters are indeed randomly generated, but I believe the purpose for this is to demonstrate the use of generate.mirt_object() function, which requires item parameters that are already known. 

I think the confusion comes from the fact that item parameters are not calculated in this example. Traditionally, in item response theory the item parameters are calculated on a data sample. The Wikipedia page for IRT has a lot of good information and the 3 parameter logistic model, for example, calculates 3 item parameters based on the probability of answering a specific question correctly. I believe the theta in that equation is the "true" ability given at the conclusion of the test. Item parameters are measured on specific populations (usually people who take the tests) and you basically just fit a logistic function over the probability of answering each item correctly (it might not be a logistic function, there are other models as well, but that one seems to be the most popular one). My understanding of IRT is that it measures the ability of the sample and then compares that ability to the following test takers, therefore updating of parameters is important feature of CATs in general that should happen every so often to make sure that the measurement are correct or as close as possible to correct. I see it as a tool to compare one to the general population (of test takers), which is why CATs usually give their results in percentiles rather than absolute marks. Once the mathematical function of choice is fitted to the data (using mirt package), you have calculated item parameters and using those you can then generate CATs (using the mirtCAT library).

I found it helpful to think about 1PL models first, where only the difficulty of an item is taken into account and then add the discrimination parameter and so on...

Hope this helps

Best wishes,
Siyan
